14: # Skill Asset File Templates - Creation Guidelines
15: 
16: Templates and guidelines for creating asset files in AI agent skills.
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: ### Location & Naming
21: 
22: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/assets/`
23: 
24: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with the appropriate extension
25: 
26: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
27: |---------------|-----------------|
28: | `frontmatter-templates.md` | `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (PascalCase) |
29: | `config-examples.yaml` | `config_examples.yaml` (snake_case) |
30: | `validation-checklist.md` | `ValidationChecklist.MD` (wrong case) |
31: | `emoji-reference.md` | `emojiReference.md` (camelCase) |
32: 
33: ### When to Create Assets
34: 
35: **Create an asset file when:**
36: - Templates users apply repeatedly
37: - Reference data >50 lines and self-contained
38: - Multiple examples of same pattern exist
39: - Lookup tables or decision matrices needed
40: - Template variations for different scenarios
41: 
42: **Keep in SKILL.md when:**
43: - Content <30 lines
44: - Tightly coupled to workflow logic
45: - Needs to be visible immediately (not progressive disclosure)
46: - Part of core instructions (RULES, WORKFLOW sections)
47: 
48: ---
49: 
50: ## 2. ASSET FILE TYPES
51: 
52: ### Template Files
53: **Purpose**: Provide copy-paste starting points for common tasks
54: 
55: **Naming**: `[content-type]-templates.md`
56: - Example: `frontmatter-templates.md`, `structure-templates.md`
57: 
58: **Structure**:
59: - One template per section
60: - Include field descriptions
61: - Show complete examples
62: - Explain when to use each template
63: 
64: **Use cases**:
65: - Document templates (SKILL.md, commands, knowledge files)
66: - Configuration templates (YAML, JSON)
67: - Code templates (functions, classes, modules)
68: 
69: ### Reference Files
70: **Purpose**: Provide lookup tables, decision trees, or reference data
71: 
72: **Naming**: `[topic]-reference.md`
73: - Example: `emoji-reference.md`, `validation-reference.md`
74: 
75: **Structure**:
76: - Tables or lists for quick lookup
77: - Decision matrices
78: - Classification systems
79: - Standards and conventions
80: 
81: **Use cases**:
82: - Emoji selection guides
83: - File type classifications
84: - Validation rule sets
85: - Naming conventions
86: 
87: ### Example Files
88: **Purpose**: Show working examples of skill outputs
89: 
90: **Naming**: `[topic]-examples.md`
91: - Example: `optimization-examples.md`, `skill-examples.md`
92: 
93: **Structure**:
94: - Before/after comparisons
95: - Annotated examples
96: - Multiple variations
97: - Anti-patterns to avoid
98: 
99: **Use cases**:
100: - Complete skill applications
101: - Common patterns
102: - Edge cases
103: - Quality standards
104: 
105: ### Guide Files
106: **Purpose**: Detailed how-to guides for complex processes
107: 
108: **Naming**: `[process]-guide.md`
109: - Example: `packaging-guide.md`, `distribution-guide.md`
110: 
111: **Structure**:
112: - Step-by-step instructions
113: - Troubleshooting sections
114: - Best practices
115: - Common pitfalls
116: 
117: **Use cases**:
118: - Multi-step processes
119: - Advanced techniques
120: - Workflow deep-dives
121: - Integration guides
122: 
123: ---
124: 
125: ## 3. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
126: 
127: ### Title and Intro
128: 
129: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
130: 
131: ```markdown
132: ---
133: title: [Title]
134: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
135: trigger_phrases:
136:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
137:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
138:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
139: importance_tier: normal
140: contextType: general
141: version: 1.0.0.0
142: ---
143: 
144: # [Title]
145: 
146: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
147: 
148: \## 1. OVERVIEW
149: 
150: ### Purpose
151: 
152: [Why this asset exists]
153: 
154: ### Usage
155: 
156: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: \## 2. [Content Section]
161: 
162: [The actual template/checklist/snippet content]
163: 
164: ---
165: 
166: ## N. Related Resources (optional, if present must be last)
167: 
168: [Links to related files]
169: 
170: ```
171: 
172: Every asset file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content, `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, and `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
173: 
174: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and OVERVIEW section.**
175: > The intro is a hook. OVERVIEW provides the details.
176: 
177: #### GOOD Intro Structure
178: 
179: ```markdown
180: # Git Commit Templates
181: 
182: Copy the template that matches the change, fill the fields, and commit.
183: 
184: \## 1. OVERVIEW
185: 
186: ### Purpose
187: 
188: Uniform messages let a reader scan history by intent instead of by author.
189: 
190: ### Usage
191: 
192: Copy the appropriate template based on commit type...
193: 
194: ---
195: 
196: \## 2. COMMIT TEMPLATES
197: ...
198: ```
199: 
200: #### BAD Intro Structure (too long, has subsections)
201: 
202: ```markdown
203: # Git Commit Templates
204: 
205: Copy-paste templates for creating well-structured commit messages.
206: 
207: ### Core Principle    ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
208: Atomic commits with clear intent = maintainable history.
209: 
210: ### When to Use       ← WRONG: This belongs in OVERVIEW section!
211: - Creating new features
212: - Fixing bugs
213: 
214: ---
215: ```
216: 
217: ### Intro vs OVERVIEW Content Placement
218: 
219: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | OVERVIEW Section       |
220: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
221: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat)    |
222: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
223: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
224: | How to copy/customize | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
225: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
226: | Any H2/H3 subsections | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES                  |
227: 
228: ---
229: 
230: ## 4. STANDARD ASSET STRUCTURE
231: 
232: **Template**:
233: 
234: ````markdown
235: ---
236: title: Asset Title - Descriptive Subtitle
237: description: One-line description of what this asset provides
238: trigger_phrases:
239:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
240:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
241:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
242: importance_tier: normal
243: contextType: general
244: version: 1.0.0.0
245: ---
246: 
247: # Asset Title - Descriptive Subtitle
248: 
249: Brief introduction (1-2 sentences) explaining what this asset provides and when to use it.
250: 
251: \## 1. OVERVIEW
252: 
253: ### Purpose
254: 
255: [Why this asset exists, what problem it solves]
256: 
257: ### Usage
258: 
259: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
260: 
261: ---
262: 
263: \## 2. SECTION NAME
264: 
265: **Key Points**:
266: - Point 1
267: - Point 2
268: - Point 3
269: 
270: **Template**:
271: ```[language]
272: # Template content here
273: # With explanatory comments
274: ```
275: 
276: **Field Guidelines**:
277: 
278: **`field_name`**:
279: - Description of field
280: - Format requirements
281: - Example: `value-example`
282: 
283: **Complete Example**:
284: ```[language]
285: # Complete working example
286: # Ready to copy and adapt
287: ```
288: 
289: ---
290: 
291: \## 3. SECTION NAME
292: 
293: [Continue pattern...]
294: 
295: ---
296: 
297: ## N. RELATED RESOURCES
298: 
299: [Links to related files - MUST be last section if present]
300: 
301: ````
302: 
303: ---
304: 
305: ## 5. LOGIC REPRESENTATION PATTERNS
306: 
307: **Purpose**: Guidelines for representing logic, workflows, and decision trees in asset files using structured formats instead of prose.
308: 
309: **Why Structured Logic?**
310: - **Clarity**: Executable-style logic is easier to understand than prose
311: - **AI-Friendly**: LLMs parse structured logic better than narrative descriptions
312: - **Maintainability**: Changes to logic are more visible in structured formats
313: - **Consistency**: Same patterns across all asset files
314: 
315: ### When to Use Each Format
316: 
317: **Use Python Pseudo-Code When:**
318: - Complex branching logic (multiple IF/ELIF/ELSE conditions)
319: - Function/method definitions with clear inputs/outputs
320: - State management or algorithmic processes
321: - Validation or transformation logic
322: - Examples: Mode detection, validation pipelines, decision functions
323: 
324: **Use YAML Structures When:**
325: - Configuration data (settings, options, parameters)
326: - Pipeline definitions (multi-step workflows with clear phases)
327: - Hierarchical workflows (nested processes)
328: - Metadata structures (categorization, tagging)
329: - Examples: Workflow definitions, configuration templates, feature matrices
330: 
331: **Use Markdown Decision Trees When:**
332: - Simple branching logic (2-5 branches)
333: - Visual flow representation (user-facing paths)
334: - Classification systems (type determination)
335: - Quick decision guides
336: - Examples: Document type selection, frontmatter requirements
337: 
338: **Keep Markdown Prose When:**
339: - Explanatory text and conceptual overviews
340: - Narrative examples with context
341: - Best practices guidance
342: - Introductions and summaries
343: 
344: ---
345: 
346: ## 6. DECISION LOGIC EXAMPLES
347: 
348: **Purpose**: Demonstrate how to convert markdown prose into structured decision logic.
349: 
350: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Mode Detection
351: 
352: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
353: ```markdown
354: Check user input for mode indicators:
355: - If "$quick" is present, use quick mode with auto-scaling depth
356: - If "$ticket" is present, use ticket mode with depth 10
357: - Otherwise, use interactive mode with depth 10
358: ```
359: 
360: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
361: ```python
362: def detect_mode(request):
363:     """Detect execution mode from user request markers"""
364: 
365:     if '$quick' in request:
366:         mode = 'quick'
367:         depth = 'auto_scale_1_to_5'
368:     elif '$ticket' in request:
369:         mode = 'ticket'
370:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
371:     else:
372:         # DEFAULT TO INTERACTIVE
373:         mode = 'interactive'
374:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
375: 
376:     return mode, depth
377: ```
378: 
379: ### Markdown Decision Tree: Frontmatter Requirements
380: 
381: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
382: ```markdown
383: Different document types have different frontmatter requirements:
384: - SKILL.md files must have frontmatter with name, description, allowed-tools, and version
385: - Command files must have frontmatter with description and argument-hint
386: - Skill reference/asset files must have the 5-field block
387: - Knowledge files outside skill folders should not have frontmatter
388: - Spec files typically don't have frontmatter
389: ```
390: 
391: **After (Markdown Decision Tree)**:
392: ```
393: Document type?
394: ├─> SKILL.md             → MUST have frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, version)
395: ├─> Command              → MUST have frontmatter (description, argument-hint, allowed-tools)
396: ├─> Skill Reference/Asset → MUST have the 5-field block (title, description,
397: │                           trigger_phrases, importance_tier, contextType)
398: ├─> Knowledge (outside skills) → MUST NOT have frontmatter (remove if present)
399: ├─> Spec                 → SHOULD NOT have frontmatter (suggest removal)
400: └─> README               → No specific requirement (usually none)
401: ```
402: 
403: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Validation Logic
404: 
405: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
406: ```markdown
407: Validate the document structure:
408: 1. Check if required sections exist
409: 2. Verify section ordering is correct
410: 3. Ensure frontmatter is valid (if present)
411: ```
412: 
413: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
414: ```python
415: def validate_document(doc, doc_type):
416:     """Validate document structure and content"""
417: 
418:     errors = []
419: 
420:     # Check required sections
421:     required_sections = get_required_sections(doc_type)
422:     for section in required_sections:
423:         if section not in doc.sections:
424:             errors.append(f"Missing required section: {section}")
425: 
426:     # Verify section ordering
427:     expected_order = get_section_order(doc_type)
428:     actual_order = [s.name for s in doc.sections]
429:     if actual_order != expected_order:
430:         errors.append(f"Section order incorrect. Expected: {expected_order}")
431: 
432:     # Validate frontmatter
433:     if doc.has_frontmatter:
434:         frontmatter_errors = validate_frontmatter(doc.frontmatter, doc_type)
435:         errors.extend(frontmatter_errors)
436: 
437:     return errors
438: ```
439: 
440: ---
441: 
442: ## 7. WORKFLOW PATTERNS
443: 
444: **Purpose**: Show how to represent multi-step workflows using YAML structures.
445: 
446: ### YAML Pipeline: Document Creation Workflow
447: 
448: **Before (Markdown List)**:
449: ```markdown
450: 1. Analyze the request and determine document type
451: 2. Select appropriate template
452: 3. Populate template with content
453: 4. Validate structure and content
454: 5. Apply formatting standards
455: 6. Run quality checks
456: ```
457: 
458: **After (YAML Pipeline)**:
459: ```yaml
460: document_creation_workflow:
461:   phase_1_analysis:
462:     action: "Analyze request and determine document type"
463:     output: "Document type classification"
464:     validation: "Type must be one of: SKILL, Command, Knowledge, Spec, README"
465: 
466:   phase_2_template_selection:
467:     action: "Select appropriate template based on document type"
468:     output: "Template file path"
469:     depends_on: "phase_1_analysis"
470: 
471:   phase_3_population:
472:     action: "Populate template with user-provided content"
473:     output: "Draft document with filled sections"
474:     depends_on: "phase_2_template_selection"
475: 
476:   phase_4_validation:
477:     action: "Validate structure, frontmatter, section ordering"
478:     output: "Validation report (errors/warnings)"
479:     depends_on: "phase_3_population"
480: 
481:   phase_5_formatting:
482:     action: "Apply code standards (spacing, headers)"
483:     output: "Formatted document"
484:     depends_on: "phase_4_validation"
485: 
486:   phase_6_quality_check:
487:     action: "Review checklist + run AI quality evaluation"
488:     output: "Quality notes and improvement recommendations"
489:     depends_on: "phase_5_formatting"
490: ```
491: 
492: ### YAML Configuration: Feature Flags
493: 
494: **Before (Markdown Table)**:
495: ```markdown
496: | Feature           | Default | Description                         |
497: | ----------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------- |
498: | strict_validation | true    | Enforce all validation rules        |
499: | auto_fix          | false   | Automatically fix formatting issues |
500: | frontmatter_check | true    | Validate frontmatter per document type |
501: ```
502: 
503: **After (YAML Configuration)**:
504: ```yaml
505: feature_flags:
506:   strict_validation:
507:     default: true
508:     description: "Enforce all validation rules without warnings"
509:     values: [true, false]
510: 
511:   auto_fix:
512:     default: false
513:     description: "Automatically fix formatting issues during validation"
514:     values: [true, false]
515:     warning: "Use with caution - may change document semantics"
516: 
517:   frontmatter_check:
518:     default: true
519:     description: "Validate frontmatter fields per document type"
520:     values: [true, false]
521:     enforcement_level: "error"
522: ```
523: 
524: ### YAML Workflow: Multi-Branch Decision Process
525: 
526: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
527: ```markdown
528: The system should detect when to generate variants:
529: - If user explicitly requests options (shows me options, variations, different approaches)
530: - If complexity is high (7+) and uncertainty signals are present (not sure, what would work)

20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose of SKILL.md Files
23: 
24: SKILL.md files define AI agent skills - reusable capabilities that extend an agent's functionality for specific domains or workflows. A well-crafted SKILL.md:
25: 
26: - **Triggers automatically** when relevant patterns are detected
27: - **Guides the agent** through specialized workflows
28: - **Maintains consistency** across conversations
29: - **Encodes expertise** in specific domains
30: 
31: ### Template Overview
32: 
33: This guide provides **one comprehensive SKILL template** (Section 3) that covers all skill types from simple single-purpose tools to complex multi-mode orchestrators.
34: 
35: **The template is flexible:**
36: - **Simple skills**: Use required core sections only (WHEN TO USE, SMART ROUTING, HOW IT WORKS, RULES, REFERENCES)
37: - **Skills with bundled resources**: Say in Section 2 what selects the skill and what it loads first, and put the router in the sibling `ROUTER.md`. Use `references/`, `assets/`, and `scripts/`
38: - **Multi-mode skills**: Expand WHEN TO USE and HOW IT WORKS sections by mode
39: - **All skills**: Section 2 (SMART ROUTING) is required: 8 to 12 non-blank lines of plain prose
40: 
41: **Target size**: 800-2000 lines for SKILL.md (<5k words total)
42: 
43: **Examples**:
44: - Simple: Unit test generator, documentation formatter (no bundled resources)
45: - Moderate: API client, specialized code reviewer (with references and assets)
46: - Complex: Workflow orchestrator, document quality pipeline (multi-mode with extensive resources)
47: 
48: ### Progressive Disclosure Principle
49: 
50: SKILL.md architecture follows progressive disclosure:
51: 
52: 1. **Metadata** (YAML frontmatter) - Always in context (~100 words)
53: 2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill activates (<5k words)
54: 3. **Bundled resources** - Loaded as needed (unlimited size)
55: 
56: **Critical**: Keep SKILL.md <5k words. Move detailed content to `references/`, `scripts/`, or `assets/`.
57: 
58: ### Document Type Requirements
59: 
60: **Enforcement Level**: STRICT (SKILL.md files require perfect structure)
61: 
62: **Required Elements**:
63: - ✅ YAML frontmatter with required fields
64: - ✅ H1 title with subtitle
65: - ✅ Numbered H2 sections (ALL CAPS, integers only, never a letter suffix such as `2b.`)
66: - ✅ Section separators (`---`)
67: - ✅ No table of contents (forbidden in SKILL.md)
68: 
69: **Quality Targets**:
70: - Structure: 100/100
71: - Content quality: High (AI-evaluated)
72: - Overall: High (human/AI judgment)

76: ## 2. FRONTMATTER REQUIREMENTS

78: ### Required Fields
79: 
80: | Field | Required | Format | Example |
81: |-------|----------|--------|---------|
82: | `name` | ✅ | hyphen-case | `my-skill-name` |
83: | `description` | ✅ | Single line, **≤ 130 chars** for skills (≤ 110 for commands), 1,536-char hard cap | `"Handles X when Y occurs"` |
84: | `allowed-tools` | ✅ | Array: `[Tool1, Tool2]` | `[Read, Write, Edit, Bash]` |
85: | `version` | ✅ | 4-part X.Y.Z.W | `1.0.0.0` |

401: 
402: The router in `ROUTER.md` discovers reference, asset, and script docs dynamically. Start with `references/[primary].md`, `assets/[template].md`, and any skill-specific automation under `scripts/`, then load task-specific resources according to Section 2.
403: 
404: Scripts: `scripts/[primary-helper]` when the skill ships automation. Omit this line when no scripts exist.
405: 
406: Related skills: `[related-skill]` for [relationship], `[other-skill]` for [relationship], and `system-spec-kit` when packet documentation or memory continuity applies.
407: 
408: Install guide: [INSTALL-GUIDE.md](INSTALL-GUIDE.md) when the skill has installation or configuration steps.
409: 
410: ---
411: 
412: **Word Count Targets**:
413: - Section 1 (WHEN TO USE): 150-200 lines
414: - Section 2 (SMART ROUTING): 8-12 non-blank lines of plain prose (the router block lives in the sibling `ROUTER.md`)
415: - Section 3 (HOW IT WORKS): 200-300 lines
416: - Section 4 (RULES): 150-200 lines
417: - Section 5 (REFERENCES): 40-120 lines
418: - Section 6 (SUCCESS CRITERIA): 80-120 lines
419: - Section 7 (INTEGRATION POINTS): 100-150 lines
420: - Section 8 (REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES): 20-60 lines
421: 
422: **Bundled Resources Structure (Monolithic)**:
423: ```
424: .skilled/skills/skill-name/       # Note: .skilled/skills/ (singular, NOT skills)
425: ├── SKILL.md (800-1000 lines)
426: └── Bundled Resources
427:     ├── scripts/          - Executable automation
428:     ├── references/       - Detailed documentation (flat or domain subfolders)
429:     └── assets/           - Templates and examples (subfolders OK)
430:         ├── opencode/     - OpenCode component templates (skills, agents, commands)
431:         └── readme/        - README-shaped scaffolds (README, install guide)
432: ```
433: 
434: **Folder Organization Principle**:
435: - **references/** = flat for small skills, domain subfolders for medium/complex skills
436:   - Flat example: `references/core-standards.md`, `references/validation.md`
437:   - Domain example: `references/backend/go/`, `references/frontend/react/`
438: - **assets/** = Subfolders ALLOWED when organizing many files by category
439:   - Group related templates together
440:   - Example: `assets/skill/`, `assets/readme/`, `assets/flowcharts/`
441: - **scripts/** = Typically flat, but subfolders OK for large script collections
442: 
443: **Native Discovery**:
444: - Skills auto-discovered from `.skilled/skills/*/SKILL.md` frontmatter
445: - Skill name in frontmatter MUST match folder name
446: - Skills appear as `skills_<name>` functions in OpenCode (hyphens → underscores)
447: - Invoke via `Read(".skilled/skills/<name>/SKILL.md")`

504: ### Section 2: SMART ROUTING (Required for All Skills)
505: 
506: **Purpose**: Use this section to explain how you route a request to this skill's resources.
507: 
508: **Three skill kinds, one shape**:
509: 
510: | Kind | How to tell | What Section 2 says |
511: |------|-------------|---------------------|
512: | Hub | the folder holds `mode-registry.json` and `hub-router.json` | how a prompt reaches a mode, and where the root `ROUTER.md` is |
513: | Mode packet | a packet folder inside a hub | what selects this packet, what it loads first, and where its own `ROUTER.md` is |
514: | Standalone | neither hub file | the same as a mode packet, with the router in its own `ROUTER.md` |
515: 
516: **The limit**: 12 non-blank lines and 180 words are the hard ceilings the check enforces. Aim for 8 to 12 lines. A packet or standalone skill says three things: what selects it, what it loads first, and where the machine router is.
517: 
518: **The sibling router**: the machine router lives in `ROUTER.md` beside `SKILL.md`, under a final `## MACHINE ROUTER` heading.
519: That heading is the one every reader parses. Its section number is optional, so `## MACHINE ROUTER` and `## 9. MACHINE ROUTER` both count, and the check ignores the number.
520: Keep pseudocode out of SMART ROUTING and put it in that section.
521: `SKILL.md` carries no `## MACHINE ROUTER` section of its own: two homes for one router is the dual declaration the check reports.
522: 
523: **The link line**: Section 2 names the router file with a relative markdown link, [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md), and its target resolves on disk. A sentence that mentions the name without a link fails, because a reader cannot follow it to a file that is not there.
524: 
525: **One router per folder**: every skill and every mode packet owns `ROUTER.md` inside its own folder, linked from its own `SKILL.md`. A router file whose real path leaves the folder is not that skill's router.
526: 
527: **The no-match outcome** is named `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` everywhere. Low confidence returns a disambiguation checklist, never an empty result and never a guess.
528: 
529: **Validation**: `package_skill.py --strict` reports the routing shape with five codes:
530: 
531: | Code | Finding |
532: |------|---------|
533: | `RS-001` | SMART ROUTING is longer than the limit (12 lines or 180 words by default) |
534: | `RS-002` | `SKILL.md` carries a `## MACHINE ROUTER` section, with or without a code block |
535: | `RS-003` | A `## MACHINE ROUTER` section is not the last H2 of the document that holds it |
536: | `RS-004` | the skill has no sibling `ROUTER.md`, or its real path leaves the skill folder |
537: | `RS-005` | `SKILL.md` has no relative markdown link to `./ROUTER.md` that resolves |
538: 
539: The machine block itself is a fenced block or an unfenced run of indented lines.
540: It declares the router with one of these markers: `INTENT_SIGNALS =`, `RESOURCE_MAP =`, `DEFAULT_RESOURCE =`, `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST =`, `def discover_markdown_resources` or `def _guard_in_skill`.
541: A fence closes only on a run of the same character that is at least as long as its opening run.
542: 
543: **Known debt** is listed in `sk-create-skill/scripts/routing-shape-known-debt.json`.
544: Entries use skill paths relative to `.skilled/skills`, such as `sk-code/sk-code-review`.
545: A folder outside that root is never debt.
546: Each entry records `{"lines", "words", "machineBlocks", "codes"}`.
547: A listed skill fails if its line count, word count or machine blocks left in `SKILL.md` exceed the record, or if it adds an unrecorded code.
548: The checker ignores entries in any other form.
549: Remove an entry when the skill follows the canon.
550: 
551: **Placement**: the SMART ROUTING section sits after Section 1 (WHEN TO USE) and before HOW IT WORKS, and `ROUTER.md` sits beside `SKILL.md` at the skill root.
552: 
553: **Worked example** (a canon Section 2 and its sibling router, nothing else):
554: 
555: \## 2. SMART ROUTING
556: 
557: Use this skill for [domain] work: [trigger 1], [trigger 2], or [trigger 3].
558: The first signal is [project/stack/mode detection], because it picks the knowledge folder before any intent scoring.
559: Load `references/[default].md` first on every run. The other files assume it.
560: Then load what the matched intent maps to: [intent A] reads `references/[domain]/[a].md`, and [intent B] reads `assets/[domain]/[b].md`.
561: Keep every path inside this skill folder and load a file only when it exists.
562: When two intents score close together, follow both in rank order.
563: When nothing matches, report `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` with the checklist from the machine router instead of guessing.
564: The machine router lives in [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md); read it before selecting a resource.
565: 
566: ---
567: 
568: The link resolves to the sibling file, whose one heading the readers parse is:
569: 
570: \## MACHINE ROUTER
571: 
572: ```python
573: DEFAULT_RESOURCE = "references/[default].md"
574: INTENT_SIGNALS = {"PRIMARY": {"weight": 4, "keywords": [("[keyword]", 4), ("[phrase]", 3)]}}
575: RESOURCE_MAP = {"PRIMARY": ["references/[domain]/[primary].md"]}
576: UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST = ["Confirm the routing key", "Confirm the intent", "Provide one concrete input"]
577: 
578: def route_[skill_name]_resources(user_request, task=None):
579:     inventory = discover_markdown_resources()
580:     primary, secondary, scores = classify_intents(user_request, task)
581:     if max(scores.values() or [0]) < 0.5:
582:         return {"load_level": "UNKNOWN_FALLBACK", "checklist": UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST}
583:     return {"routing_key": get_routing_key(task, [primary]), "resources": inventory}
584: ```
585: 
586: The full resilience pattern (guarded paths, recursive discovery, routing keys) is in [skill-smart-router.md](./skill-smart-router.md).
587: 
588: **Writing Tips**:
589: - Open Section 2 with the signal that actually picks this skill's files.
590: - Name the first file to load, so a reader knows where to start.
591: - Name the router file with a markdown link, so a reader can open it.
592: - Keep `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` as the named no-match outcome.
593: - Edit `INTENT_SIGNALS` and `RESOURCE_MAP` in `ROUTER.md` when the skill gains a domain.
594: - Avoid duplicate lookup tables, static file inventories, and unguarded `load()` calls.
595: 
596: **Word Budget**: 8-12 non-blank lines of prose

14: # SKILL.md File Templates - Creation Guide
15: 
16: Templates for creating SKILL.md files with proper structure, frontmatter, and required sections.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose of SKILL.md Files
23: 
24: SKILL.md files define AI agent skills - reusable capabilities that extend an agent's functionality for specific domains or workflows. A well-crafted SKILL.md:
25: 
26: - **Triggers automatically** when relevant patterns are detected
27: - **Guides the agent** through specialized workflows
28: - **Maintains consistency** across conversations
29: - **Encodes expertise** in specific domains
30: 
31: ### Template Overview
32: 
33: This guide provides **one comprehensive SKILL template** (Section 3) that covers all skill types from simple single-purpose tools to complex multi-mode orchestrators.
34: 
35: **The template is flexible:**
36: - **Simple skills**: Use required core sections only (WHEN TO USE, SMART ROUTING, HOW IT WORKS, RULES, REFERENCES)
37: - **Skills with bundled resources**: Say in Section 2 what selects the skill and what it loads first, and put the router in the sibling `ROUTER.md`. Use `references/`, `assets/`, and `scripts/`
38: - **Multi-mode skills**: Expand WHEN TO USE and HOW IT WORKS sections by mode
39: - **All skills**: Section 2 (SMART ROUTING) is required: 8 to 12 non-blank lines of plain prose
40: 
41: **Target size**: 800-2000 lines for SKILL.md (<5k words total)
42: 
43: **Examples**:
44: - Simple: Unit test generator, documentation formatter (no bundled resources)
45: - Moderate: API client, specialized code reviewer (with references and assets)
46: - Complex: Workflow orchestrator, document quality pipeline (multi-mode with extensive resources)
47: 
48: ### Progressive Disclosure Principle
49: 
50: SKILL.md architecture follows progressive disclosure:
51: 
52: 1. **Metadata** (YAML frontmatter) - Always in context (~100 words)
53: 2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill activates (<5k words)
54: 3. **Bundled resources** - Loaded as needed (unlimited size)
55: 
56: **Critical**: Keep SKILL.md <5k words. Move detailed content to `references/`, `scripts/`, or `assets/`.
57: 
58: ### Document Type Requirements
59: 
60: **Enforcement Level**: STRICT (SKILL.md files require perfect structure)
61: 
62: **Required Elements**:
63: - ✅ YAML frontmatter with required fields
64: - ✅ H1 title with subtitle
65: - ✅ Numbered H2 sections (ALL CAPS, integers only, never a letter suffix such as `2b.`)
66: - ✅ Section separators (`---`)
67: - ✅ No table of contents (forbidden in SKILL.md)
68: 
69: **Quality Targets**:
70: - Structure: 100/100
71: - Content quality: High (AI-evaluated)
72: - Overall: High (human/AI judgment)
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## 2. FRONTMATTER REQUIREMENTS
77: 
78: ### Required Fields
79: 
80: | Field | Required | Format | Example |
81: |-------|----------|--------|---------|
82: | `name` | ✅ | hyphen-case | `my-skill-name` |
83: | `description` | ✅ | Single line, **≤ 130 chars** for skills (≤ 110 for commands), 1,536-char hard cap | `"Handles X when Y occurs"` |
84: | `allowed-tools` | ✅ | Array: `[Tool1, Tool2]` | `[Read, Write, Edit, Bash]` |
85: | `version` | ✅ | 4-part X.Y.Z.W | `1.0.0.0` |
86: 
87: > **Hard rules**: not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside the skill's `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects that the dispatch preflight reads.
88: 
89: > **Description budget & trim style**: see [`frontmatter-templates.md` § Description Budget & Trim Style](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md).
90: > Keep total project descriptions under the ~6,400-character ceiling. This leaves headroom below the 8,000-character auto-discovery limit.
91: > Drop product and stack lists. Drop marketing prose. Keep the skill name, primary verb, domain noun and mode suffixes (`:auto` or `:confirm`).
92: 
93: ### Template
94: 
95: ```yaml
96: ---
97: name: sk-example
98: description: Example workflow skill demonstrating proper frontmatter format with specific capabilities, use cases, and key differentiators for AI agent discovery.
99: allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep]
100: version: 1.0.0.0
101: ---
102: ```
103: 
104: ### Key Rules
105: 
106: - **name**: Must match folder name exactly, hyphen-case only
107: - **description**: Third-person voice, single line, no `<>` brackets
108: - **allowed-tools**: Use brackets `[...]`, not comma-separated string
109: - **hard rules**: Not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects the dispatch preflight reads.
110: 
111: > **Complete Reference**: For validation rules, edge cases, array formats, and all document type frontmatter, see [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md)
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 3. SKILL TEMPLATE (WITH BUNDLED RESOURCES)

118: 
119: **Target**: 800-2000 lines (SKILL.md <1000 lines, rest in resources)

128: - `package_skill.py` fails if `REFERENCES` is missing and no approved combined `SMART ROUTING & REFERENCES` structure exists.

138: allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep]

504: ### Section 2: SMART ROUTING (Required for All Skills)
505: 
506: **Purpose**: Use this section to explain how you route a request to this skill's resources.
507: 
508: **Three skill kinds, one shape**:
509: 
510: | Kind | How to tell | What Section 2 says |
511: |------|-------------|---------------------|
512: | Hub | the folder holds `mode-registry.json` and `hub-router.json` | how a prompt reaches a mode, and where the root `ROUTER.md` is |
513: | Mode packet | a packet folder inside a hub | what selects this packet, what it loads first, and where its own `ROUTER.md` is |
514: | Standalone | neither hub file | the same as a mode packet, with the router in its own `ROUTER.md` |
515: 
516: **The limit**: 12 non-blank lines and 180 words are the hard ceilings the check enforces. Aim for 8 to 12 lines. A packet or standalone skill says three things: what selects it, what it loads first, and where the machine router is.
517: 
518: **The sibling router**: the machine router lives in `ROUTER.md` beside `SKILL.md`, under a final `## MACHINE ROUTER` heading.
519: That heading is the one every reader parses. Its section number is optional, so `## MACHINE ROUTER` and `## 9. MACHINE ROUTER` both count, and the check ignores the number.
520: Keep pseudocode out of SMART ROUTING and put it in that section.
521: `SKILL.md` carries no `## MACHINE ROUTER` section of its own: two homes for one router is the dual declaration the check reports.
522: 
523: **The link line**: Section 2 names the router file with a relative markdown link, [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md), and its target resolves on disk. A sentence that mentions the name without a link fails, because a reader cannot follow it to a file that is not there.
524: 
525: **One router per folder**: every skill and every mode packet owns `ROUTER.md` inside its own folder, linked from its own `SKILL.md`. A router file whose real path leaves the folder is not that skill's router.
526: 
527: **The no-match outcome** is named `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` everywhere. Low confidence returns a disambiguation checklist, never an empty result and never a guess.
528: 
529: **Validation**: `package_skill.py --strict` reports the routing shape with five codes:
530: 
531: | Code | Finding |
532: |------|---------|
533: | `RS-001` | SMART ROUTING is longer than the limit (12 lines or 180 words by default) |
534: | `RS-002` | `SKILL.md` carries a `## MACHINE ROUTER` section, with or without a code block |
535: | `RS-003` | A `## MACHINE ROUTER` section is not the last H2 of the document that holds it |
536: | `RS-004` | the skill has no sibling `ROUTER.md`, or its real path leaves the skill folder |
537: | `RS-005` | `SKILL.md` has no relative markdown link to `./ROUTER.md` that resolves |
538: 
539: The machine block itself is a fenced block or an unfenced run of indented lines.
540: It declares the router with one of these markers: `INTENT_SIGNALS =`, `RESOURCE_MAP =`, `DEFAULT_RESOURCE =`, `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST =`, `def discover_markdown_resources` or `def _guard_in_skill`.
541: A fence closes only on a run of the same character that is at least as long as its opening run.
542: 
543: **Known debt** is listed in `sk-create-skill/scripts/routing-shape-known-debt.json`.
544: Entries use skill paths relative to `.skilled/skills`, such as `sk-code/sk-code-review`.
545: A folder outside that root is never debt.
546: Each entry records `{"lines", "words", "machineBlocks", "codes"}`.
547: A listed skill fails if its line count, word count or machine blocks left in `SKILL.md` exceed the record, or if it adds an unrecorded code.
548: The checker ignores entries in any other form.
549: Remove an entry when the skill follows the canon.
550: 
551: **Placement**: the SMART ROUTING section sits after Section 1 (WHEN TO USE) and before HOW IT WORKS, and `ROUTER.md` sits beside `SKILL.md` at the skill root.
552: 
553: **Worked example** (a canon Section 2 and its sibling router, nothing else):
554: 
555: \## 2. SMART ROUTING
556: 
557: Use this skill for [domain] work: [trigger 1], [trigger 2], or [trigger 3].
558: The first signal is [project/stack/mode detection], because it picks the knowledge folder before any intent scoring.
559: Load `references/[default].md` first on every run. The other files assume it.
560: Then load what the matched intent maps to: [intent A] reads `references/[domain]/[a].md`, and [intent B] reads `assets/[domain]/[b].md`.
561: Keep every path inside this skill folder and load a file only when it exists.
562: When two intents score close together, follow both in rank order.
563: When nothing matches, report `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` with the checklist from the machine router instead of guessing.
564: The machine router lives in [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md); read it before selecting a resource.
565: 
566: ---
567: 
568: The link resolves to the sibling file, whose one heading the readers parse is:
569: 
570: \## MACHINE ROUTER
571: 
572: ```python
573: DEFAULT_RESOURCE = "references/[default].md"
574: INTENT_SIGNALS = {"PRIMARY": {"weight": 4, "keywords": [("[keyword]", 4), ("[phrase]", 3)]}}
575: RESOURCE_MAP = {"PRIMARY": ["references/[domain]/[primary].md"]}
576: UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST = ["Confirm the routing key", "Confirm the intent", "Provide one concrete input"]
577: 
578: def route_[skill_name]_resources(user_request, task=None):
579:     inventory = discover_markdown_resources()
580:     primary, secondary, scores = classify_intents(user_request, task)
581:     if max(scores.values() or [0]) < 0.5:
582:         return {"load_level": "UNKNOWN_FALLBACK", "checklist": UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST}
583:     return {"routing_key": get_routing_key(task, [primary]), "resources": inventory}
584: ```
585: 
586: The full resilience pattern (guarded paths, recursive discovery, routing keys) is in [skill-smart-router.md](./skill-smart-router.md).
587: 
588: **Writing Tips**:
589: - Open Section 2 with the signal that actually picks this skill's files.
590: - Name the first file to load, so a reader knows where to start.
591: - Name the router file with a markdown link, so a reader can open it.
592: - Keep `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` as the named no-match outcome.
593: - Edit `INTENT_SIGNALS` and `RESOURCE_MAP` in `ROUTER.md` when the skill gains a domain.
594: - Avoid duplicate lookup tables, static file inventories, and unguarded `load()` calls.
595: 
596: **Word Budget**: 8-12 non-blank lines of prose

14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141: 
142: Frontmatter is optional for normal project READMEs and recommended for skill or system documentation that should be discoverable.
143: 
144: ```yaml
145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:
149:   - "[search phrase]"
150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.
155: 
156: ---
157: 
158: ## 6. FILLABLE SCAFFOLD
159: 
160: Copy this scaffold, then remove sections that do not apply.
161: 
162: ````markdown

186: | Version | [Version or release channel] |
187: | Main audience | [Who uses this] |
188: | Operating modes | [Mode count or short list] |

191: 
192: | Capability | This Project | Related Option |
193: |---|---|---|
194: | [Capability] | [Current behavior] | [Difference] |
195: 
196: 
197: ---
198: 
199: ## 2. QUICK START
200: 
201: ```bash
202: # Install or prepare
203: [command]
204: 
205: # Verify
206: [command]
207: ```
208: 
209: Expected result: [what success looks like].
210: 
211: 
212: ---
213: 
214: ## 3. FEATURES
215: 
216: ### Key Features
217: 
218: | Feature | What It Does |
219: |---|---|
220: | [Feature] | [Current behavior] |
221: 
222: 
223: ---
224: 
225: ## 4. REQUIREMENTS
226: 
227: | Requirement | Minimum | Notes |
228: |---|---|---|
229: | [Runtime or tool] | [Version] | [Why it is needed] |
230: 
231: 
232: ---
233: 
234: ## 5. STRUCTURE
235: 
236: ```text

238: +-- [path]/        # [Purpose]
239: `-- [file]         # [Purpose]
240: ```
241: 
242: | Path | Purpose |
243: |---|---|
244: | `[path]` | [Role] |
245: 
246: <!-- For items needing more than one line, use the itemized pattern
247:      from Section 4 instead of this table. -->
248: 
249: 
250: ---
251: 
252: ## 6. CONFIGURATION
253: 
254: | Option | Default | Purpose |
255: |---|---|---|
256: | `[OPTION]` | `[value]` | [What it controls] |
257: 
258:

260: 
261: ## 7. USAGE EXAMPLES
262: 
263: ```bash

265: ```
266:

268: 
269:

271:

273:

275: |---|---|---|
276: | [Symptom] | [Cause] | [Action] |
277: 
278: 
279: ---

281: ## 9. FAQ
282:

284:

286:

288: ---

292: ### Related Skills
293:

298: ### Related Documents
299: 
300: | Document | Purpose |
301: |---|---|
302: | [`[Document]`](./path/to/doc.md) | [Why it matters] |
303: 
304: ````
305:

307: 
308: ## 7. VALIDATION CHECKLIST
309: 
310: - [ ] README type is correct. Code folders use `readme-code-template.md`.
311: - [ ] Included sections match the audience and task.

317: - [ ] HVR passes: no em dashes, semicolons, banned words or setup phrases.

13: 
14: # sk-create-goal
15: 
16: > Write the goal.md a spec packet is missing, from that packet's own documents, and leave session goal state alone.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
21: 
22: | Aspect | What you get |
23: |---|---|
24: | **Use it for** | Authoring or revising a packet `goal.md` through six operations: top-level, phase-parent, child, retrofit, phase-add and amend |
25: | **Invoke with** | `/create:goal <packet path> [operation] [:auto|:confirm]`, or a plain request to author a packet goal |
26: | **Works on** | An existing spec packet with its own `spec.md` and its own acceptance criteria where the level requires them |
27: | **Produces** | One goal filled from the template for its kind and the packet's sources, plus the parent chat slice for the operator |
28: | **Never touches** | Session objective state. A request to set, bind or resend a goal goes to the goal hooks |
29: 
30: ---
31: 
32: ## 2. OVERVIEW
33: 
34: ### What The Mode Does
35: 
36: `sk-create-goal` turns a packet's own specifications into its `goal.md`. Every goal starts from one of three templates, for a top-level packet, a phase parent or a phase child, and is filled with one objective sentence, the frozen decisions later work must honor and three to seven completion criteria. Each criterion resolves to an exit code, a count or a named artifact. Each template is a checked copy of the system-spec-kit goal template, and a test fails when the two drift apart.
37: 
38: A phase parent also gets a binding table with exactly one row per direct phase-child folder. The table lives only in the phase-parent goal. Each row points at that child's `goal.md`, and the child goal is then authoritative for its own phase.
39: 
40: ### The File And Session Boundary
41: 
42: The mode authors files. It never sets, binds, injects or resends a session objective, and it never tracks whether an operator has done so. After a parent goal changes, the mode prints the file-derived `chat_slice` from `goal.cjs` and stops. The operator holds that slice as the objective. The goal hooks, or the host's native goal command, own everything past the print.
43: 
44: ### Where The Content Comes From
45: 
46: Goal content is derived from the packet's own documents, never from a remembered summary. A nested child goal uses only that child's own specification and acceptance criteria. A phase parent's objective and criteria come from the parent-level sources, and its binding table is compared with the phase folders on disk by name, not by count.
47: 
48: ---
49: 
50: ## 3. WHEN TO USE
51: 
52: ### Use This Mode When
53: 
54: - A top-level packet or phase parent needs a goal, or a revised one.
55: - A nested phase child needs its own goal.
56: - An existing packet has no `goal.md` at all and needs one added.
57: - A new phase appears in the phase map and on disk and needs one binding row plus its child goal.
58: - A parent goal runs over the 4,000-character durable budget and must be cut without losing a criterion.
59: - You want a parent goal's chat slice printed for the operator.
60: 
61: ### When Not To Use
62: 
63: - The target packet does not exist. Create it with system-spec-kit first.
64: - The packet's phase structure is not settled. Plan the phases with system-spec-kit first.
65: - The request is to set, bind, inject or resend a session objective. That is goal-hook work, or the host's native goal command. This mode redirects it and writes nothing.
66: - The request changes runtime goal behavior or system-spec-kit template tooling. Those owners stay outside this mode.
67: 
68: ---
69: 
70: ## 4. THE SIX OPERATIONS
71: 
72: | Operation | Use it when |
73: |---|---|
74: | `top-level` | The target is a top-level packet and its goal is being authored or revised |
75: | `phase-parent` | The target has direct phase-child folders and its parent goal, binding table included, is being authored or revised |
76: | `child` | A nested phase child needs a goal written from its own sources |
77: | `retrofit` | An existing packet of any shape has no `goal.md` yet |
78: | `phase-add` | A phase was added and needs exactly one parent binding row and its child goal |
79: | `amend` | An existing goal must change, including a parent amendment driven by a child change |
80: 
81: An operation that alters a parent decision or criterion amends the parent first, then updates the child. A child goal never overrides a parent decision.
82: 
83: ---
84: 
85: ## 5. HOW IT WORKS
86: 
87: 1. **Read the sources.** The packet's own `spec.md` and `acceptance-criteria.md`. For a phase parent, the Phase Documentation Map and every direct phase-child directory. For a nested child, only that child's own documents.
88: 2. **Route.** File content or session state? What role does the packet play? Does `goal.md` exist? Does a child change force a parent amendment? A session-state request is redirected and nothing is written.
89: 3. **Start from the template.** Copy the block from [`goal-top-level-template.md`](./assets/goal-top-level-template.md), [`goal-phase-parent-template.md`](./assets/goal-phase-parent-template.md) or [`goal-phase-child-template.md`](./assets/goal-phase-child-template.md) into `goal.md`. 14: # Goal Authoring Standards
15: 
16: ## 1. OVERVIEW
17: 
18: The goal template defines the structure. These checks ask whether an authored goal states its purpose and records fixed choices. They also give a reader a way to judge completion. The [Human Voice Rules](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md) govern the prose.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 2. OBJECTIVE
23: 
24: Rule: Write one sentence that says what the packet exists to accomplish. State its purpose. Leave methods and progress out.
25: 
26: Failure it prevents: A template placeholder or work update does not tell the reader what the packet is for.
27: 
28: Reader check: Can you tell what the packet exists to accomplish from this sentence alone, without reading a method or progress report? Yes or no.
29: 
30: Example: "Produce ten iterations of evidence-cited research on a numbered, searchable commit grammar for sk-git, on how a per-commit identifier is minted without collisions across branches, and on how 9,106 commits are rewritten and their citations remapped safely." (`specs/sk-git/028-crawlable-commit-history/001-research/goal.md:43`)
31: 
32: ---
33: 
34: ## 3. DECISIONS
35: 
36: Rule: Record the frozen choices that later work must honor. State each so a reader can test work against it. Changing a choice requires an amendment.
37: 
38: Failure it prevents: Unstated or movable choices let later work drift without a visible decision to change.
39: 
40: Reader check: Can you test later work against each listed choice, and would changing one require an amendment? Yes or no.
41: 
42: Example: "This phase produces findings only. No file outside research/ changes." (`specs/sk-git/028-crawlable-commit-history/001-research/goal.md:53`)
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 4. COMPLETION CRITERIA
47: 
48: Rule: Write three to seven criteria. Each criterion resolves to one observable result. It may state a command's exit code or a count. It may instead name an artifact. Keep every criterion checkable without opening another file, then copy the criteria verbatim into the objective.
49: 
50: Failure it prevents: A vague criterion or a check that depends on another file leaves completion open. A count that conflicts with the declared scope gives two different completion targets.
51: 
52: Reader check: Does the goal contain three to seven self-contained criteria with an explicit result, and does the objective repeat them verbatim? Yes or no.
53: 
54: Example: "research/lineages/deepseek/deep-research-state.jsonl holds 10 iteration records" (`specs/sk-git/028-crawlable-commit-history/001-research/goal.md:75`). This criterion names an artifact and a count.
55: 
56: ---
57: 
58: ## 5. LOG
59: 
60: Rule: Record progress, evidence, deviations and findings only in the volatile log below the durable slice. Keep temporary status out of the objective, decisions and criteria.
61: 
62: Failure it prevents: Progress in the durable directive becomes stale as the work changes and can mislead a later reader about the packet's purpose or completion.
63: 
64: Reader check: Are all progress updates, evidence, deviations and findings below the log heading, with none in the durable directive? Yes or no.
65: 
66: Example: The progress row "| Phase opened | Pending | |" appears in the log (`specs/sk-git/028-crawlable-commit-history/001-research/goal.md:94`).
67: 
68: ---
69: 
70: ## 6. VOICE
71: 
72: Rule: Apply the Human Voice Rules to every sentence you author. Use plain, direct wording and support claims with specific evidence. Link to the voice standard instead of copying it here.
73: 
74: Failure it prevents: Vague or inflated prose hides what the packet requires and weakens the reader's ability to test its claims.
75: 
76: Reader check: Does each authored sentence read plainly under the Human Voice Rules, with claims backed by specific evidence? Yes or no.
77: 
78: Example: "This phase produces findings only. No file outside research/ changes." (`specs/sk-git/028-crawlable-commit-history/001-research/goal.md:53`)
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: ## 7. FRONTMATTER
83: 
84: Rule: Keep the frontmatter to key-value lines between its opening and closing `---` fences, with no other `---` line inside it.
85: 
86: Failure it prevents: The frontmatter closes at its first `---` line after the opener. An inner one ends it early, and the keys after it reach the durable slice and the chat slice as goal text, where they count against the 4,000-character budget.
87: 
88: Reader check: Does the file hold exactly two `---` lines above its first heading, the opener and the closer? Yes or no. `check-goal.cjs` reports a break as a `frontmatter-fence` finding.
89: 
90: Example: The frontmatter opens at line 1 and closes at line 27, with no fence line between them (`specs/sk-git/028-crawlable-commit-history/001-research/goal.md:1-27`).

38: Failure it prevents: Unstated or movable choices let later work drift without a visible decision to change.
39: 
40: Reader check: Can you test later work against each listed choice, and would changing one require an amendment? Yes or no.
41: 
42: Example: "This phase produces findings only. No file outside research/ changes." (`specs/sk-git/028-crawlable-commit-history/001-research/goal.md:53`)
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 4. COMPLETION CRITERIA
47: 
48: Rule: Write three to seven criteria. Each criterion resolves to one observable result. It may state a command's exit code or a count. It may instead name an artifact. Keep every criterion checkable without opening another file, then copy the criteria verbatim into the objective.
49: 
50: Failure it prevents: A vague criterion or a check that depends on another file leaves completion open. A count that conflicts with the declared scope gives two different completion targets.
51: 
52: Reader check: Does the goal contain three to seven self-contained criteria with an explicit result, and does the objective repeat them verbatim? Yes or no.
53: 
54: Example: "research/lineages/deepseek/deep-research-state.jsonl holds 10 iteration records" (`specs/sk-git/028-crawlable-commit-history/001-research/goal.md:75`). This criterion names an artifact and a count.
55: 
56: ---
57: 
58: ## 5. LOG
59: 
60: Rule: Record progress, evidence, deviations and findings only in the volatile log below the durable slice. Keep temporary status out of the objective, decisions and criteria.
61: 
62: Failure it prevents: Progress in the durable directive becomes stale as the work changes and can mislead a later reader about the packet's purpose or completion.
63: 
64: Reader check: Are all progress updates, evidence, deviations and findings below the log heading, with none in the durable directive? Yes or no.
65: 
66: Example: The progress row "| Phase opened | Pending | |" appears in the log (`specs/sk-git/028-crawlable-commit-history/001-research/goal.md:94`).
67: 
68: ---
69: 
70: ## 6. VOICE
71: 
72: Rule: Apply the Human Voice Rules to every sentence you author. Use plain, direct wording and support claims with specific evidence. Link to the voice standard instead of copying it here.
73: 
74: Failure it prevents: Vague or inflated prose hides what the packet requires and weakens the reader's ability to test its claims.
75: 
76: Reader check: Does each authored sentence read plainly under the Human Voice Rules, with claims backed by specific evidence? Yes or no.
77: 
78: Example: "This phase produces findings only. No file outside research/ changes." (`specs/sk-git/028-crawlable-commit-history/001-research/goal.md:53`)
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: ## 7. FRONTMATTER
83: 
84: Rule: Keep the frontmatter to key-value lines between its opening and closing `---` fences, with no other `---` line inside it.
85: 
86: Failure it prevents: The frontmatter closes at its first `---` line after the opener. An inner one ends it early, and the keys after it reach the durable slice and the chat slice as goal text, where they count against the 4,000-character budget.
87: 
88: Reader check: Does the file hold exactly two `---` lines above its first heading, the opener and the closer? Yes or no. `check-goal.cjs` reports a break as a `frontmatter-fence` finding.
89: 
90: Example: The frontmatter opens at line 1 and closes at line 27, with no fence line between them (`specs/sk-git/028-crawlable-commit-history/001-research/goal.md:1-27`).

13: # Goal Budget and Handoff
14: 
15: ## 1. OVERVIEW
16: 
17: Use the packet report to check a top-level goal or phase parent. Keep every completion criterion when cutting an over-budget parent. Section 2 is the one rule for which goals carry the cap, section 3 the one full cut order and section 4 the one full rule for what a parent goal sent in chat contains. Other documents point here rather than restating them.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 2. MEASURE THE DURABLE SLICE
22: 
23: Run this command from the repository root:
24: 
25: ```bash
26: node .skilled/hooks/goal/bin/goal.cjs packet <packet> --workspace <repo root>
27: ```
28: 
29: Replace the placeholders with the packet path and repository root. Read `packet_durable_chars` and `packet_budget` in the output. The count covers text after the closing frontmatter fence and before the log anchor. Anchors and comments inside that range count. The manifest sets the limit to 4,000 characters for top-level packets and phase parents. A count of 4,000 is within budget. A larger count reports `packet_budget=over`. ([manifest, lines 24 to 28](../../../system-spec-kit/templates/spec-kit-docs.json))
30: 
31: The packet command prints the count and budget state with the other packet fields. ([packet output, lines 205 to 218](../../../../hooks/goal/bin/goal.cjs)) The shared module measures the durable slice from the frontmatter boundary to the log anchor. ([slice measurement, lines 57 to 68](../../../../hooks/goal/lib/goal-slice.cjs))
32: 
33: The cap applies to a top-level packet and to any folder that is itself a phase parent, meaning it has phase children or its `spec.md` declares the phase level, even when that folder sits inside another packet. Only a phase child that is not itself a phase parent is exempt, and its packet report reads `packet_budget=unknown`. `goal.cjs packet`, `check-goal.cjs` and `validate.sh` draw this same line. An applicable goal can also report `unknown` if the budget manifest is missing or invalid. Treat that result as unverified and resolve the manifest issue before judging the goal. ([budget resolution, lines 288 to 307](../../../../hooks/goal/lib/goal-slice.cjs) and [applicability and state, lines 400 to 415](../../../../hooks/goal/lib/goal-slice.cjs))
34: 
35: ---
36: 
37: ## 3. CUT IN THIS ORDER
38: 
39: When a parent exceeds 4,000 characters, cut in this order and rerun the packet command after the cuts.
40:

## 5. MACHINE ROUTER

The hub's detailed routing prose, moved here from `SKILL.md` so the skill body keeps only a short routing summary and a pointer to this file. It sits last, after the stage-two map above, and it declares no map of its own: the `INTENT_SIGNALS` and `RESOURCE_MAP` block in section 3 stays the only replay source.

### Surface Router — per-intent leaf sets

Stage 2 of routing lives in section 3 of this file.
It defines three things:
- The per-intent leaf model: document quality, optimization, skill creation, parent-hub creation, agent creation, command creation, the paired agent-plus-command lane, the human-voice pass, playbooks, playbook conversations, feature catalogs, READMEs, changelogs, benchmarks, diffs, frontmatter, packet goals, repo rules, and the explicit full-toolkit intent.
- The machine-readable `INTENT_SIGNALS` / `RESOURCE_MAP` block that the deterministic router-replay and benchmarks parse.
- The how-to-read rules: a dominant intent gives one leaf set, near-tied intents give a deduped union, and no keyword match gives the hub UNKNOWN fallback, never a silent default.

Every `RESOURCE_MAP` path is packet-qualified or an authored shared-alias disk path, and each converts to the canonical `(workflowMode, leafResourceId)` pair at the one contract boundary.

The reason this file stays a separate document from `SKILL.md` and from `hub-router.json` is in [the parent-skill reference](sk-create-skill/references/parent-skill/parent-skills-nested-packets.md#why-the-leaf-router-stays-in-routermd).
---- AGENTS 210-222

## 5. 🧭 TOOLS, SEARCH & MCP ROUTING

| Tool | Purpose |
| ------| ---------|
| **Trigger index + retrieval conventions** | Gate 1 answers from the committed trigger index. Free text uses the ripgrep recipes in `system-spec-kit/references/retrieval/retrieval-conventions.md`, over spec docs and skill docs only. A miss is a clean no-hit. Scope and declared losses: `system-spec-kit` SKILL.md §3. |
| **Git (sk-git)** | Worktree setup, conventional commits and PR creation. Mechanics: `.skilled/skills/sk-git/`. |

#### Git Workspace Safety

- **Never choose the workspace yourself, and never create a branch with git primitives.** When a git workspace trigger fires, ask the operator to choose **A) Create a git worktree** or **B) Work on current branch**, and wait. Branches come only from `sk-git`'s commands.
- **Ask before every push to a branch outside sk-git's remote allowlist.** A prior approval never carries forward. An explicit push instruction is itself the go-ahead.
---- playbook 52-66

---

## 3. WHY THE CRITERIA ARE COPIED

Nothing dereferences a path inside an objective string. Every goal surface in this repository is string-in, string-out: the working agent can open the file because it has tools, but whatever judges completion sees only the stored string.

Leave the criteria in the file alone and the evaluator is judging a table of contents. Copy them and it can judge the packet. This is the one duplication the design accepts. The rules for writing criteria that survive the copy are section 4 of `sk-create-goal`'s [authoring-standards.md](../../../sk-doc/sk-create-goal/references/authoring-standards.md).

---

## 4. WHEN IT WILL NOT FIT

The validator fails a parent past 4,000 durable characters. That is the one limit, with no warning tier below it, so a parent under 4,000 needs no cutting. Which goals carry it is section 2 of [budget-and-handoff.md](../../../sk-doc/sk-create-goal/references/budget-and-handoff.md): a child is unbounded unless it is itself a phase parent. When a parent is over, cut it in the order section 3 of [budget-and-handoff.md](../../../sk-doc/sk-create-goal/references/budget-and-handoff.md) gives, which is the one full cut order.

# create-frontmatter

> The block at the top of every document in this repository follows one contract. This is where that contract lives.

---

## 1. AT A GLANCE

| Aspect | What you get |
|---|---|
| **Use it for** | Authoring a frontmatter block, fixing a rejected one, or deriving a `version` |
| **Invoke with** | "what frontmatter does this need", a validator rejection, or a direct read of `SKILL.md` |
| **Works on** | Any document class in the repository, plus the files the version standard puts out of scope |
| **Produces** | A correct block, a specific fix, or a derived 4-part version |
| **Does not produce** | The document itself, or a change to a validator |

---

## 2. OVERVIEW

### Why This Skill Exists

Frontmatter is small and it is load-bearing. The advisor routes on `trigger_phrases`. Discovery drops a skill whose `description` pushes the project over a shared character budget, and it drops it silently. A missing `version` fails a corpus gate. None of that is visible in the document body, so a wrong block looks like a working document right up until something stops finding it.

Six modes in this hub emit frontmatter and every one of their templates defers to the same specification. Until now that specification sat in the hub's shared tier, which is the right reach and the wrong ownership. Shared means anyone may read it. It also meant nobody was accountable for it, so it drifted from the validators that enforce it and no single mode could be asked to fix that.

This mode is the answer to "who owns frontmatter."

### What It Owns, And What It Does Not

It owns the **rules**: which fields a class carries, what each field may contain, the description budget and its trim style, and the derivation of the 4-part `version`.

It also owns the **value lists** for `contextType` and `importance_tier`, in `assets/frontmatter-values.json`. spec-kit's validator and save code, sk-doc's `validate_document.py` and the skill-advisor checker all read that one file, so a value added there is legal everywhere at once. The list of session context types a save payload uses is not frontmatter, and stays in spec-kit.

It does not own the **enforcement**. Three scripts do that, and all three stay in the hub's shared tier: the versioning engine, the corpus gate that wraps it, and the fast validator that four command workflows call. They stay because a post-edit hook outside this hub resolves one of them by literal path on every qualifying edit. Moving them would break a runtime hook to gain a tidier diagram.

The split is worth stating plainly, because it decides where to go with a question. **The mode owns the contract, the shared tier keeps the enforcement.** If you want to know what a validator is checking for, read here. If you want to change how it checks, that is a shared-tier change and the contract moves first.

### Document Class Is The First Question

Almost every rejected block is a field that one class requires and another forbids. Read in isolation the field looks right, which is why reading the field row before the class row wastes the most time.

Skill manifests carry a name and an allowed-tools list. References and assets carry a five-field block the advisor harvests. Commands and agents carry frontmatter too and are deliberately outside the version standard. Spec documents use inline metadata instead of a block at all.

---

# Frontmatter Versioning Standard

Every skill doc carries a 4-part `version: X.Y.Z.W` field in its frontmatter. On `SKILL.md` it names the skill edition and equals the newest changelog entry. On every other doc it names that doc's own edition: a new doc starts at `1.0.0.0`, and any change to its body raises it. This reference is the single source of truth for the format, the scope, the bump rule and how the field is enforced.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW AND SCOPE

### In scope (MUST carry `version`)

Every Markdown doc under `.skilled/skills/**` that has a frontmatter block:

| Doc | Version it carries |
|-----|--------------------|
| `SKILL.md`, at a skill root or a mode-packet root | The skill edition, anchored to the changelog (Section 3) |
| Every other doc: READMEs, references, assets, feature catalogs, testing playbooks, `ROUTER.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `INSTALL-GUIDE.md`, hook docs and the rest | Its own edition, raised by the bump rule (Section 4) |

### Out of scope

| Class | Why |
|-------|-----|
| Changelog entries (`changelog/**`) | They keep the version of the release they record, which `package_skill.py` checks |
| Test input: anything under a `tests/` or `fixtures/` folder | A fixture is shaped like a doc but is input to a test, and a test may compare its bytes |
| Generated output and runtime internals: anything under `runtime/`, `benchmark/` or `behavior-benchmark/`, unless a `references/`, `assets/`, `feature-catalog/` or `manual-testing-playbook/` folder sits above the file | Reports, corpora and code-folder notes are produced or owned by their tooling. A catalog or playbook inside a runtime folder is still authored, so it stays in |
| Filled spec-folder examples under `templates/examples/` | They carry system-spec-kit's spec-doc frontmatter, not a skill doc's |
| A doc with no frontmatter block, such as the style corpus | Every check skips it, and a versioning pass never synthesizes a block |

# Frontmatter Versioning Standard

Every skill doc carries a 4-part `version: X.Y.Z.W` field in its frontmatter. On `SKILL.md` it names the skill edition and equals the newest changelog entry. On every other doc it names that doc's own edition: a new doc starts at `1.0.0.0`, and any change to its body raises it. This reference is the single source of truth for the format, the scope, the bump rule and how the field is enforced.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW AND SCOPE

### In scope (MUST carry `version`)

Every Markdown doc under `.skilled/skills/**` that has a frontmatter block:

| Doc | Version it carries |
|-----|--------------------|
| `SKILL.md`, at a skill root or a mode-packet root | The skill edition, anchored to the changelog (Section 3) |
| Every other doc: READMEs, references, assets, feature catalogs, testing playbooks, `ROUTER.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `INSTALL-GUIDE.md`, hook docs and the rest | Its own edition, raised by the bump rule (Section 4) |

### Out of scope

| Class | Why |
|-------|-----|
| Changelog entries (`changelog/**`) | They keep the version of the release they record, which `package_skill.py` checks |
| Test input: anything under a `tests/` or `fixtures/` folder | A fixture is shaped like a doc but is input to a test, and a test may compare its bytes |
| Generated output and runtime internals: anything under `runtime/`, `benchmark/` or `behavior-benchmark/`, unless a `references/`, `assets/`, `feature-catalog/` or `manual-testing-playbook/` folder sits above the file | Reports, corpora and code-folder notes are produced or owned by their tooling. A catalog or playbook inside a runtime folder is still authored, so it stays in |

| A doc with no frontmatter block, such as the style corpus | Every check skips it, and a versioning pass never synthesizes a block |
| `.skilled/scratch/`, `node_modules/`, `dist/` | Not docs |

`.skilled/commands/*.md` and `.skilled/agents/*.md` are governed separately: a command's `version` stays optional, and an agent carries none.

---

Exactly four dot-separated non-negative integers, validated by `^\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+$`. A value may be quoted (`version: "1.2.0.0"`); the check reads the value inside the quotes, and a raise keeps them.

# YAML Frontmatter Templates - Document Type Reference

Templates and validation rules for YAML frontmatter by document type.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

### What Is YAML Frontmatter?

**YAML frontmatter** is a metadata block at the beginning of markdown files, delimited by `---` markers. It provides machine-readable configuration that controls how AI agents and tools process the document.

```yaml
---
name: skill-name
description: What this skill does
allowed-tools: Read, Write, Bash
---

# Document Content Starts Here
```

**Core Purpose**:
- **Tool configuration** - Define which AI tools a skill/command can use
- **Discovery** - Enable programmatic listing and searching of skills/commands
- **Argument parsing** - Specify expected inputs for commands
- **Metadata storage** - Version, category, tags for organization

**Key Difference from Inline Metadata**:
- YAML frontmatter = Machine-parseable, strict format, at file start
- Inline metadata = Human-readable, flexible format, anywhere in document

34: 3. Write one objective sentence that states the packet's purpose. Record decisions that later work must honor. Add three to seven self-contained completion criteria based on the acceptance criteria. Repeat those criteria verbatim in the evaluator-facing objective text required by the goal contract.
35: 4. Keep progress and temporary findings below the goal's log heading. A top-level goal has no binding section.

39: ```bash
40: bash .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/cli/spec/validate.sh <packet> --strict
41: node .skilled/hooks/goal/bin/goal.cjs packet <packet> --workspace "$PWD"

51: 
52: 1. Read the phase parent's `spec.md`, its `acceptance-criteria.md` when present and the complete Phase Documentation Map. Record each direct phase folder named by the map.

70: node .skilled/hooks/goal/bin/goal.cjs packet <packet> --workspace "$PWD"
71: ```

87: ! grep -q '<!-- ANCHOR:binding -->' <child>/goal.md
88: ```

96: ### Retrofit a missing goal
97: 
98: Treat adding a goal to an existing packet that has none as its own operation. First confirm the packet exists, its role is clear and its source documents are present. Do not call this operation when a goal already exists. Revise that file instead.
